Types of Cherries & Berries: A 16-Fruit Guide for Chefs and Bartenders

Knowledge Guide • Fruit • By Nigel A. Thomas, Hospitality Executive • October 2026

Cherries and berries are some of the most valuable, most photogenic and most perishable ingredients in a hotel or restaurant. A tray of perfect raspberries lifts a dessert; the same tray a day too late is a loss. Knowing exactly what you are buying – how it should look, how it should taste, what it is good for and how to choose it – is basic professional knowledge for every chef, pastry cook, bartender and F&B manager.

This guide covers sixteen fruits: sweet and sour cherries, the familiar berries (strawberry, blueberry, blackberry, raspberry), the tart ones (cranberry, redcurrant, blackcurrant, gooseberry, lingonberry), the soft dark ones (boysenberry, mulberry, elderberry) and two special ingredients (cloudberry and açaí berry). Each entry follows the same four-point check – appearance, flavour, best uses and selection – with extra notes for the kitchen and bar. A free poster of the whole guide is at the end of the article.

What Counts as a Berry?

In everyday kitchen language, a berry is any small, soft, juicy fruit. Botanists are stricter. Blueberries, cranberries, lingonberries, currants and gooseberries are true berries. Cherries are stone fruit (drupes), each with a single hard pit. Strawberries are an accessory fruit, while raspberries, blackberries, boysenberries and cloudberries are aggregates of tiny drupelets, and a mulberry is a cluster of small fruits. Açaí is a small palm fruit. None of this changes how you cook, but it explains why they behave differently: aggregates and clusters are delicate and leak easily, while true berries such as blueberries and cranberries are firmer and keep longer.

How to Buy Cherries and Berries

  1. Use your eyes first. Look for bright, even colour, a natural gloss or bloom, and fresh green stems or caps where the fruit has them.
  2. Check the bottom of the box. Stains, crushed fruit and moisture at the base mean leakage and mould are coming. Reject the whole container if the bottom layer is wet.
  3. Choose dry fruit. Surface moisture speeds up spoilage. Dry, firm fruit lasts longest.
  4. Smell it. Ripe berries smell fragrant. A sour, fermented or musty smell means the fruit is overripe or mouldy.
  5. Buy to your usage. Delicate fruit such as raspberries, mulberries and strawberries should be ordered in small, frequent quantities. Cranberries, blueberries and lingonberries are hardier and can be stocked for longer.

Storage, Handling and Preparation

Store cold and dry. Keep fresh cherries and berries refrigerated, unwashed, in shallow containers in a single layer if you can. Line the container with absorbent paper and keep it lightly covered. Remove any mouldy fruit at once, because mould spreads quickly through the container.

Wash at the last moment. Rinse gently under cool running water just before use, drain on paper and use promptly. Washing early encourages spoilage. Blueberries should not be washed until needed, so that the natural bloom stays intact.

Prepare correctly. Pit cherries with a pitter, hull strawberries after washing, top and tail gooseberries and blackcurrants, strip redcurrants and elderberries from their stems with a fork, and strain coulis through a fine sieve if you want to remove seeds.

Freeze smartly. Most berries freeze well. Spread them on a tray in a single layer until solid, then bag them. Frozen fruit suits cooking, baking, smoothies and sauces better than fresh service, because the texture softens when it thaws.

Handle with clean hands and tools. Use clean boards and utensils, keep fruit away from raw meat and fish, and never return fruit that has been served to the walk-in.

The Fruits

Each entry below begins with the four-point check from the poster, then adds practical notes for the kitchen and bar.

1. Sweet Cherry

Prunus avium | Stone fruit

  • Appearance: Deep red to nearly black; plump and glossy
  • Flavor: Sweet, juicy and mildly tart
  • Best uses: Fresh service, fruit platters, cakes, compotes and garnishes
  • Selection: Choose firm fruit with fresh green stems

In the kitchen and bar: Varieties such as Bing, Lambert and the yellow-red Rainier all count as sweet cherries. Keep them refrigerated and unwashed, and rinse just before service. Cherries are stone fruit, so either pit them for desserts and drinks or warn guests that stones are present. Leave the stem on when the cherry is a garnish. Chocolate, almond, vanilla and duck are classic partners. Preserved cocktail cherries are a different product from fresh fruit.

2. Sour Cherry

Prunus cerasus | Stone fruit

  • Appearance: Bright red, smaller and softer
  • Flavor: Sharp, tangy and aromatic
  • Best uses: Pies, preserves, sauces, syrups and baking
  • Selection: Choose bright, unbruised fruit; use quickly

In the kitchen and bar: Montmorency and Morello are the best-known types. They are usually too sharp to eat raw in quantity, but cooking with sugar brings out a deep, aromatic flavour. Sour cherries suit pies, strudel, sauces for duck and game, and cherry soup. They are fragile, so buy only what you can use within a day or two, or use pitted frozen fruit.

3. Strawberry

Fragaria | Aggregate accessory fruit

  • Appearance: Bright red, heart-shaped with green cap
  • Flavor: Sweet, fragrant and gently tart
  • Best uses: Desserts, salads, smoothies, jams and garnish
  • Selection: Choose dry, firm berries with even red color

In the kitchen and bar: Botanically the strawberry is not a true berry, but every kitchen treats it as one. Store them unwashed in a single layer, rinse briefly just before use and hull afterwards, because soaking turns them watery. Macerating with a little sugar draws out juice for sauces and coulis. Cream, balsamic vinegar, basil and sparkling wine all pair well. Strawberries are a common allergen, so mention them on menus.

4. Blueberry

Vaccinium | True berry

  • Appearance: Blue-purple with a natural silvery bloom
  • Flavor: Mildly sweet with balanced acidity
  • Best uses: Breakfast, muffins, sauces, salads and smoothies
  • Selection: Choose firm, dry berries with intact bloom

In the kitchen and bar: The silvery bloom is a natural wax coating and a sign of freshness, so do not wash blueberries until you use them. Wild lowbush berries are smaller and more intensely flavoured than cultivated highbush ones. They freeze very well, and frozen berries added straight to batter, without thawing, bleed less colour into muffins and pancakes.

5. Blackberry

Rubus | Aggregate fruit

  • Appearance: Glossy black-purple clusters of drupelets
  • Flavor: Rich, juicy, sweet and pleasantly tart
  • Best uses: Desserts, jams, sauces, smoothies and garnish
  • Selection: Choose plump, dark berries without leakage

In the kitchen and bar: Each berry is a cluster of tiny drupelets, which is why it is juicy and seedy. It is very perishable, so store in a single shallow layer and use quickly. Strain a coulis if you want to remove the seeds. Apple, lemon, sage and almond complement it, and the Bramble cocktail is a classic use at the bar.

6. Raspberry

Rubus idaeus | Aggregate fruit

  • Appearance: Soft red hollow berries with fine drupelets
  • Flavor: Fragrant, delicate, sweet and tangy
  • Best uses: Pastries, coulis, salads, drinks and decoration
  • Selection: Choose dry, bright berries with no bruising

In the kitchen and bar: Raspberries are hollow because the core stays on the plant when they are picked, which is also why they are so fragile. Never stack them deeper than one or two layers. Golden and black varieties exist as well as red. Raspberry coulis is a staple in a pastry kitchen, and it finishes classics such as pavlova and peach melba.

7. Cranberry

Vaccinium macrocarpon | True berry

  • Appearance: Small, round and glossy deep-red berries
  • Flavor: Firm, sharply tart and mildly bitter
  • Best uses: Sauces, juices, baking, relish and preserves
  • Selection: Choose firm berries that bounce when fresh

In the kitchen and bar: Cranberries are very high in acid and pectin, so sauces set naturally. They are sold fresh in autumn and winter, frozen all year, and dried (usually sweetened) or as juice. They are rarely eaten raw. Simmer with sugar and orange for a classic sauce for turkey and roast meats, and use juice in drinks such as the Cosmopolitan.

8. Redcurrant

Ribes rubrum | True berry

  • Appearance: Tiny translucent red berries in hanging clusters
  • Flavor: Bright, tart and lightly sweet
  • Best uses: Jelly, sauces, desserts, salads and garnish
  • Selection: Choose shiny, firm berries on fresh green stems

In the kitchen and bar: Redcurrants hang in strings called strigs. Run a fork down the stem to remove the berries, or leave a small strig whole as an elegant garnish. They are rich in pectin, which makes them ideal for jelly. Redcurrant jelly and Cumberland sauce accompany lamb, game and paté, and the berries also go into summer pudding.

9. Blackcurrant

Ribes nigrum | True berry

  • Appearance: Small, glossy black berries in loose clusters
  • Flavor: Bold, tart, earthy and highly aromatic
  • Best uses: Cordials, jams, sauces, desserts and baking
  • Selection: Choose plump, firm berries with fresh stems

In the kitchen and bar: Blackcurrant is intensely flavoured and rarely eaten raw. It is rich in vitamin C and gives its name to crème de cassis, the liqueur in a Kir. Top and tail the berries before cooking, and sweeten well. Cordials, sorbets, jams and sauces for duck all make good use of it.

10. Gooseberry

Ribes uva-crispa | True berry

  • Appearance: Round green berries with pale vertical veins
  • Flavor: Crisp and sharply tart when young; sweeter when ripe
  • Best uses: Pies, fools, preserves, chutneys and sauces
  • Selection: Choose firm, dry fruit with smooth intact skin

In the kitchen and bar: Gooseberries are usually green, though red and yellow types exist. Snip off the stalk and the dried flower end (topping and tailing) before cooking, and cook with sugar. Gooseberry fool, crumbles and pies are classics, and a tart gooseberry sauce is a traditional partner for oily fish such as mackerel. Elderflower pairs with them beautifully.

11. Boysenberry

Rubus hybrid | Aggregate fruit

  • Appearance: Large, soft, deep maroon-purple berry clusters
  • Flavor: Juicy, rich, sweet-tart and fragrant
  • Best uses: Jams, pies, syrups, desserts and smoothies
  • Selection: Choose dark, plump berries without crushing

In the kitchen and bar: The boysenberry is a hybrid of the blackberry family, developed in California in the early twentieth century. The berries are large and soft and do not travel well, so outside growing regions you will mostly meet them frozen, as purée or in jam. They suit pies, syrups and sauces where their rich, winey flavour can shine.

12. Mulberry

Morus | Multiple fruit

  • Appearance: Elongated clustered berries, red to purple-black
  • Flavor: Sweet, juicy and gently tangy
  • Best uses: Fresh service, jam, pies, sauces and drinks
  • Selection: Choose ripe, soft berries without leakage

In the kitchen and bar: Mulberries look like elongated blackberries and range from white to red to nearly black. Ripe fruit is extremely soft and keeps for a very short time, so use it the day it arrives. The juice stains linen, uniforms and hands badly, so plan service accordingly. Jam, pies, sauces and fresh service with yoghurt or ice cream all work.

13. Elderberry

Sambucus | Small dark berries

  • Appearance: Tiny purple-black berries in broad hanging clusters
  • Flavor: Tart, earthy and mildly sweet when cooked
  • Best uses: Syrups, preserves, sauces and cooked desserts
  • Selection: Choose fully dark clusters; cook before serving

In the kitchen and bar: Raw elderberries, along with the leaves and stems, can cause nausea and stomach upset, so they must always be cooked before serving. Strip the berries from the stems, simmer them and then use them in syrups, cordials, preserves and sauces. Elderberry is a different ingredient from elderflower, which is used for its floral flavour.

14. Lingonberry

Vaccinium vitis-idaea | True berry

  • Appearance: Small, round, glossy bright-red berries
  • Flavor: Sharp, tart and lightly sweet
  • Best uses: Preserves, sauces, baking and savory pairings
  • Selection: Choose firm, vivid berries without soft spots

In the kitchen and bar: Lingonberries are closely associated with Scandinavian cooking, most famously served as a sweet-tart preserve alongside meatballs. They are also excellent with game, roast meats and rich patés, where the acidity cuts through fat. They are similar to cranberries but smaller and slightly sweeter in flavour.

15. Cloudberry

Rubus chamaemorus | Aggregate fruit

  • Appearance: Golden-orange segmented berry shaped like a raspberry
  • Flavor: Juicy, tart-sweet and gently floral
  • Best uses: Jam, desserts, sauces, yogurt and pastry
  • Selection: Choose ripe amber fruit that is soft but intact

In the kitchen and bar: Cloudberries grow wild in cold northern bogs and are prized and expensive. They turn from red to amber as they ripen. Outside the Nordic countries you will most often find them as jam, preserves or liqueur, so treat the fresh fruit as a special ingredient. Serve with cream, waffles, yoghurt or simple pastry.

16. Açaí Berry

Euterpe oleracea | Palm fruit

  • Appearance: Small, round, deep-purple berries from palm clusters
  • Flavor: Earthy, mildly tart with subtle cocoa notes
  • Best uses: Purées, smoothie bowls, drinks and frozen desserts
  • Selection: Commonly available frozen or as unsweetened purée

In the kitchen and bar: Açaí comes from a palm native to the Amazon region and spoils quickly after picking, so it is almost always sold as frozen pulp, purée or powder. Choose unsweetened products and control the sugar yourself. Blend it for smoothie bowls, drinks and frozen desserts, and add fresh fruit, granola or nuts on top.

Using Berries Across the Hotel

Bar. Berries give colour, flavour and garnish to cocktails and mocktails. Muddle blueberries, blackberries and raspberries, shake strawberries with citrus, use cranberry juice in drinks such as the Cosmopolitan, and finish glasses with a cherry or a small strig of redcurrants. Crème de cassis from blackcurrants is the base of a Kir. See the Halloween cocktails and Christmas mocktails pages for ideas.

Pastry. Coulis, compotes, tarts, cakes, pavlovas and ice creams all depend on good fruit. Match the fruit to the job: delicate raspberries for decoration, sour cherries and blackcurrants for cooking, and frozen fruit for purées.

Hot kitchen. Cranberry, lingonberry and redcurrant sauces and jellies cut through the richness of roast meats, game, duck and pâté. Gooseberry sauce pairs with oily fish. Sour cherry sauce suits duck.

Breakfast and healthy menus. Fresh berries, compotes, smoothies and açaí bowls are popular at breakfast buffets and in health-conscious menus. Keep fresh fruit chilled on ice at the buffet and replace small amounts often instead of leaving a large bowl out.

Costing, Yield and Waste

Berries are expensive and perishable, so waste control matters. Cost fruit by edible yield rather than purchase weight: cherries lose weight to stones and stems, strawberries to hulls, and currants to stalks. Use the best-looking fruit for presentation and the slightly softer fruit for sauces, purées and jams. Rotate stock first in, first out, check deliveries on arrival and keep a record of rejected fruit for supplier discussions. Frozen berries are a sensible choice for cooked dishes and smoothies, because the price is steadier and there is far less waste.

Food Safety and Allergens

Elderberries must be cooked. Raw elderberries, leaves and stems can make people ill. Never serve them raw, and remove all stems before cooking.

Stones and pits. Cherry stones are a choking and dental hazard. Pit cherries for desserts and drinks, or tell guests when stones remain. Do not crush stones into food.

Frozen berries. Frozen berries have been linked to outbreaks of hepatitis A in several countries. Buy from approved suppliers, follow supplier guidance, and heat the fruit when serving young children, older guests, pregnant guests or anyone with a weakened immune system.

Washing and cross-contamination. Wash fresh fruit in clean water just before use, keep it away from raw meat and fish, and use separate boards and knives.

Allergies. Strawberries, cherries and other fruit can trigger allergic reactions in some people. Ask guests about allergies, and declare ingredients clearly on menus.

Staining. Mulberry, blackcurrant, elderberry and blackberry juice stain linen and uniforms. Train staff to blot rather than rub, and keep a stain remover available.

Frequently Asked Questions

What is the difference between sweet and sour cherries?

Sweet cherries are eaten fresh and used for platters, desserts and garnish. Sour cherries are firmer in acidity and softer in texture, and are mainly cooked in pies, preserves, sauces and syrups.

Why are raspberries hollow?

The central core stays on the plant when the berry is picked, leaving a hollow cup. This is why raspberries are so delicate and why they should never be stacked deep.

Should I wash berries as soon as I buy them?

No. Store them dry and unwashed, and rinse them just before use. Early washing adds moisture and speeds up mould and softening.

What is the white coating on blueberries?

It is a natural waxy bloom that protects the fruit. It is a sign of freshness, and it is best left in place until the berries are used.

Can I use frozen berries instead of fresh?

Yes, for cooking, baking, purées, sauces and smoothies. Frozen fruit softens when thawed, so it is less suitable for garnish and plated fresh service. Follow your supplier's and local food-safety guidance.

Is elderberry the same as elderflower?

No. Elderflower is the blossom of the same plant and is used for its floral flavour. Elderberries are the dark fruit and must always be cooked before serving.
